In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the impact of climate variability (i.e. drought) on the NPP of different land covers and (2) the reaction of NPN, WUE and GUE to drought conditions in Sudan and Ethiopia using remote sensing and GIS techniques.

the inter-annual variation of these indicators is driven by the drought of a time scale of 3 months in the case of Ethiopia and by precipitation in the case of Sudan.
the NPP of the different land covers in Sudan and Ethiopia is sensitive to drought at time scale of three and six months.
the land cover types of Ethiopia are more vulnerable to climate variability, and thus to climate change than their counterparts in the Sudan.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NPP and the efficiency of its use of water and carbon in Sudan are more stable than those in Ethiopia.
NPP is the most sensitive to precipitation and temperature variations and that WUE and CUSE are more sensitive to drought than to variation in precipitation.
the NPP of savannah and grasslands are the most sensitive to drought in the study area.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NPP, CUE, WUE are sensitive to climate variability, and that the sensitivity varies with the type of land cover and the time scales of drought.
